# grit

A from-scratch LLM agent harness. Thesis: **no manual context-window management**. Every
turn is a durable DBOS workflow, and its context window is a projection of long-term memory
in Postgres (messages, end-of-turn summaries, and code context from the LSP), drawn at a
boundary and carried, append-only, until the next
([ADR 0052](docs/decisions/0052-a-window-is-drawn-from-the-store-at-a-boundary-and-carried-append-only-until-the-next.md)).
Nothing is carried forward as an unbounded transcript: at the limit the window is cleared and
re-projected, never slid. The same engine runs in three modes: a
local TUI harness, a cloud agent driven from Slack, and triggered tasks. Edges reach it
only through Postgres ([ADR 0002](docs/decisions/0002-edges-reach-the-engine-through-postgres.md)).

Scala 3 · Mill · `dev.dbos:transact` · Postgres 18 with `pg_textsearch` · capture checking on, and separation
checking everywhere but `grit.tui` ([ADR 0003](docs/decisions/0003-durable-is-exclusive-under-separation-checking.md)). Versions live in
`build.mill` and `.mill-version`.

## Architecture

Context is not a scrollback buffer; it is a queryable store, and what goes to the model is
a **computed projection** of that store. Three traits carry the whole design:

- `EntryStore` — append-only, never rewritten
- `ContextAssembler` — the projection; *the* trait the thesis hangs on
- `Provider` — the model call

Retrieval, summaries and LSP code context are all future `ContextAssembler`
implementations; the relevance check is the turn's own move between the assembler's reads
([ADR 0040](docs/decisions/0040-a-turn-draws-its-window-in-recorded-steps-and-only-candidates-judged-relevant-are-packed.md)),
so that signature is the real design work; everything else swaps behind it. The database transaction is a scoped, non-escaping capability (`Tx`) — capture
checking rejects any attempt to let it outlive its block.

Mill modules, and what each may name. A module's folder follows ADR 0021's three questions
(`core/`, `extensions/`, `kit/`, `deployments/`, `eval/`; [`docs/extending.md`](docs/extending.md)),
while its Mill name, package and artifact stay `grit.<name>`. More on each: `scripts/scout
area`, and the README in its folder (package order, and what the code cannot say).

| Module | Packages | Depends on | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `grit.core` | `grit.core.*` | prose | the domain and the traits; no DBOS, no JDBC driver on its classpath |
| `grit.dbos` | `sql`, `workflow`, `engine`, `internal` | core | the DBOS quarantine: DBOS, JDBC, Postgres, `schema.sql`; `internal` is lent to the eval harness alone |
| `grit.prose` | `form`, `markdown` | — | prose as edge-neutral blocks, read from markdown; each edge renders them |
| `grit.tui` | `model`, `components`, `wire`, `runtime` | core | the terminal UI library; core only from `components`/`runtime` |
| `grit.tui.examples` | `grit.tui.examples` | tui | runnable demos |
| `grit.act` | `phase`, `moves` | core | what an actor's moves do (ADR 0034), the steps the turn, jobs and the lifecycle share; names core alone |
| `grit.turn` | `grit.turn` | core, act | the durable turn's body, and a turn read back from the steps it recorded |
| `grit.lifecycle` | `transcript`, `close`, `settle`, `stitch`, `triage`, `shadow`, `post` | core, act | the engine's workflows besides the turn; their asks are moves |
| `grit.job` | `run`, `clock` | core, act | jobs (ADR 0029): a job's run, and the clock edge that starts it; names no `grit.turn` |
| `grit.digest` | `grit.digest` | core | the hello-world plugin |

| `grit.mcp` | `wire`, `scope`, `github`, `client`, `drive`, `edge` | core, edge | MCP servers and Drive's REST API: a declared service's read-only tools at its service place (ADR 0017) |

| `grit.eval.harness` | `stats` … `main` | core, dbos, turn, assembly, lifecycle, models, eval | the eval harness, run only through `scripts/eval` |
| `grit.kit` | `deployment`, `environment`, `run` | core, dbos, act, turn, job, lifecycle, assembly, models, tools, host | what a deployment is built against (ADR 0021) |
| `grit.app` | `config`, `main` | kit, digest, remind, knowledge, chat, slack, mcp, formats, host, edge | the reference deployment: the chat TUI, `grit serve`, `grit backfill` |

Mill `moduleDeps` are transitive, so `grit.kit` and `grit.app` see `dev.dbos.*` through
`grit.dbos` — enola's rule, not the compiler, guards it. Working in `extensions/tui/`? Read
[`extensions/tui/CLAUDE.md`](extensions/tui/CLAUDE.md) first.

**Changing a workflow's steps** (names, order, output encodings) must replay every history
of the current epoch: guard it with `Durable.patch`, or start a new `Turn.Epoch`
([ADR 0004](docs/decisions/0004-workflows-evolve-by-patch-within-a-compatibility-epoch.md)).
`TurnReplayTests` and `LifecycleReplayTests` are the gate.

## Reading the code

Read Scala through scout first: the `scout` MCP server, or `scripts/scout` (a native binary built
outside this repository; the script says where it looks). It answers from the compiler's TASTy, in
less text than a file read, and works in any worktree (`--root`). How to use it, what not to read
and how to edit from its text: [`.claude/rules/reading-scala.md`](.claude/rules/reading-scala.md),
which loads when a `.scala` file is first touched. Metals is for the editor
([`docs/editor-tooling.md`](docs/editor-tooling.md)).

## Style rules

Full rationale in [`STYLE.md`](STYLE.md).

These are not preferences; elision soundness depends on them. **A signature without a
capability is a promise of purity.**

1. Referentially transparent by default.
2. Effects are capabilities in the signature — `(using Tx)`, explicit `Provider`. No
   ambient singletons, no hidden I/O.
3. Expected failure in the return type (`Either`/sealed ADT). Exceptions only for the
   unrecoverable — **DBOS records a step that throws** and rethrows it on every replay,
   so a stray exception becomes that workflow's permanent result.
4. Total over partial — no `.get`, `.head`, `Map.apply`, inexhaustive matches.
5. Illegal states unrepresentable — sealed ADTs, opaque id types.
6. No `null` outside a quarantine module (rule 8).
7. Immutable data; mutation only in scoped locals.
8. **Java libraries are quarantined by role.** Each lives only in the module whose job
   needs it, translated into grit's conventions there; such modules depend only on core and
   meet only in `grit.kit` and `grit.app`. Nothing outside `grit.dbos` imports `dev.dbos.*` or `java.sql.*`,
   nothing outside `grit.models` and `grit.mcp` imports `java.net.http.*`, nothing outside `grit.slack` imports
   `com.slack.*`, nothing outside `grit.formats` imports `org.apache.pdfbox.*`, and nothing outside
   `grit.host` starts a process.
9. Explicit capability parameters over clever inference.
10. **The elision test** — if assembly dropped the body and kept only the signature and
    its doc, could a competent agent still call it correctly? If not, fix the signature.
    Trustworthy signatures let the next change be built from them alone, in far fewer tokens.
    Scaladoc says *what*, never *how*. An invariant a doc states is a missing type; a doc
    never restates what the type or visibility says; it does state every failure a caller
    can see and every constant that changes behaviour.
11. **Escape hatches carry their proof.** Every `caps.unsafe` use states beside it why the
    untracked effect cannot be observed.

**Tests** ([`STYLE.md`](STYLE.md#tests)): a test is seen red for the right reason before
it is trusted (the procedure is the `grit-test-cycle` skill's); a name states a contract
and its assertion pins the value; a fake shares one spec with the implementation it stands
in for. The `test-janitor` agent reviews test files against these rules.

## Build and format

Build, test and gate with `scripts/check`: a suite or module while iterating
(`scripts/check grit.core.agenda.AgendaTests`), bare once at a commit; `./mill grit.<module>.compile`
for whether it type-checks; format with `./mill mill.scalalib.scalafmt.ScalafmtModule/reformatAll
__.sources`. Everything else, and the procedure: the `grit-test-cycle` and `grit-local-db` skills.

Braces, never significant indentation — `-no-indent` makes it a compile error.

**Three kinds of suite.** `test` modules need nothing outside the JVM; `it` modules run
against Postgres and DBOS through `scripts/it`, which needs Docker, with no skip; `probes`
modules pin what capture and separation checking reject.

**Capture and separation checking:** [`docs/capture-checking.md`](docs/capture-checking.md)
has every trap met so far, how to test that something does not compile, and the upgrade
checklist: search it for the error when one appears.

Every warning the build enables is an error (`-Werror`), and a warning joins the set in its
own commit.

## The architecture gate (enola)

```bash
bash scripts/fetch-enola.sh    # pinned, sha256-verified, into tools/ (gitignored)
bash scripts/enola-law.sh      # regenerate, lint the declarations, check the law, fail on a cycle between production packages
```

`mcp-arch.yaml` is the walk config, `enola-intent.yaml` is the law. It is also an MCP
server — prefer `impact_analysis`, `explore`, `traverse` and `find_path` over re-deriving
structure by grepping.

**The trust boundary is not negotiable.** enola's Scala extractor dropped and mis-nested
symbols under capture syntax while reporting `parse_errors: 0`, up to 0.4.24. 0.4.29 reads the
controlled fixture correctly, but its receipt would be as silent about a new regression.
Re-measured before every version bump (`scripts/fetch-enola.sh`).

- **Import-edge and module facts are sound** and may gate. Every rule in the law is of this kind.
- **Symbol facts never gate** (`exported-surface`, `complexity-outliers`, any symbol count).
  They may guide exploration (`impact_analysis`, `explore`); a symbol-level claim is confirmed
  with scout before it is stated.

**A green gate is not automatically a checked gate.** A declaration that matches nothing
passes vacuously and `lint` still exits 0; `enola-law.sh` greps for that. A rule is not
adopted until it has been watched failing on a planted breach. The known traps are
commented in `enola-intent.yaml`. New rules are a planned session, not an aside.

## How grit's work is planned

grit plans itself with grit. Milestones, plans, stages, mechanism notes and the backlog are
artifacts of the project `grit` in a grit deployment, `planner` (its own repository, beside this
one), on the database `grit_planner`, kept under the `projects` plugin's method
([ADR 0049](docs/decisions/0049-a-projects-method-is-versioned-data-whose-checks-are-compiled-in-and-a-project-is-one-value-held-to-its-export-by-a-round-trip-law.md)).
They are read and written only through it: `bin/planner <command> '<json>'` in that repository,
or its MCP server's tools (`project_list`, `project_show`, `project_find`, `project_keep`,
`project_move`, `project_history`, …). A project artifact is not a claude.ai Artifact. There are no
planning files in this repository.

- **Start of a session:** the artifact a session or subagent type is working on is claimed for its
  slot, and a SessionStart or SubagentStart hook injects that artifact's brief. Read what it cites
  before acting; the brief names the process that governs the work.
- **During the work:** the store is updated as part of the work, not after it: a step is not done
  until its artifact's state says so. An idea that surfaces mid-task becomes a `note`, not part of
  the change.
- **Databases:** `grit` is a person's own and off limits to agents; an agent's runs use its own
  database, and `grit_planner` is durable: never reset or dropped (the `grit-local-db` skill).

This is a first step toward a modality grit is built for: a repository whose coordination and
feature work go through a grit deployment, later with a coding sandbox, so that grit's own
subagents write code beside developer-driven harnesses like Claude Code.

## Working agreements

- **Verify against the source, not the summary.** Three claims in this project's original
  design synthesis turned out to be wrong because they summarized *around* the reference
  material instead of reading its APIs. `javap` the jar; read the current docs. A claim
  becomes a design constraint only after it has been checked.
- **Park, don't widen.** An idea that surfaces mid-task goes into the backlog, not into
  the current change.
- **A design decision that clears the ADR threshold gets a record** in
  [`docs/decisions/`](docs/decisions/README.md), the same turn it is made. Most don't clear
  it: their rationale belongs in a comment beside the code or in the commit message.
- **Plan before implementing.** A roadmap item, or any change to a core trait, a library API
  or behaviour a person sees, starts with a short plan and waits for Nick's go. The plan
  says what changes, the alternatives turned down, how it will be verified (including the
  real-use run below), and what is parked. It has an **Elision section**: every new or
  changed public signature with its Scaladoc as it will be written, whether a caller could
  use it from those alone (rule 10), and what that check changed in the design. This one
  question has produced most of a refactor's design improvements. It also has a **Capture
  and separation section**: which values hold capabilities and which must be pure, what
  each new trait or type parameter may capture, where a step body or a transaction must
  not reach (the `Durable`, a `Tx` escaping), any `caps.unsafe` with its proof (rule 11),
  and for each claim the compiler is meant to enforce, the probe that shows it rejects the
  breach ([`docs/capture-checking.md`](docs/capture-checking.md)). It has a **Sharing
  section**: for each new type, trait or function, the existing one it reuses or the second
  caller it serves, and each near-copy of existing code the change would add, folded into one
  place instead. A new type's name is searched for its synonyms in the codebase: where one
  names a kin idea, the plan says why grit needs two, or uses the one it has. Of two designs
  that pass the elision test, the one that shares more code wins: one implementation that a
  turn, a job and a rehearsal all run beats two kept alike by hand.
  Mechanical edits, doc corrections and small fixes inside an agreed plan need none of these.
- **Package layout is designed, not accreted.** A new module, library or package starts
  with its layout in the plan: each package one idea, named for it; no source file at a
  group's root; the packages in a one-way dependency order, written down where the module
  is documented (`extensions/tui/CLAUDE.md` is the pattern). A module that is one idea is one
  package; when it grows a second, it becomes subpackages, none of its files left at the
  root. A layout that has drifted gets redesigned, not patched. The law fails on a new
  import cycle; the rest is review.
- **Done includes a real-use run** for anything a person interacts with, such as the TUI,
  a CLI or an edge. Use the real model, restart mid-turn, and wait as long as a person
  would. Tests that read the model rather than the painted screen, or that run against the
  stub, have passed paint and latency bugs.
- **Commit points.** Commit when a planned item, or a self-contained step inside one, has
  its tests passing with no warnings and the law green. Don't ask first; report the hash.
  One item per commit, never two mixed. Work reaches `main` through a pull request; never
  push to `main` directly, and never amend or rewrite history on it.
- **One home per fact.** State a fact in one place and link to it from the others. No
  counts in docs: test totals, check counts and rule counts go in commit messages, where
  they are true as of that commit.
- **LLM spend stays under a few cents per run** of anything that calls a real model, such
  as a live test, a probe or a real-use run. Use a cheap model and a small `max_tokens`,
  and say what a run cost. Neither test tier makes model calls.

Text inside <grit_note> is a note from grit, not from the person and not a tool's answer. Follow it as you follow this prompt.

tools.name: read_hidden
tools.description: Shows in full something your request shows only as a note ("Hidden here as h1: …"): what it says comes back as this call's answer. After you read it, you can't do what that note says you'd lose until you've answered. Read it when your answer needs what it says.

name.description: The name its note gives, such as h1.

tools.name: extract
tools.description: It can only answer yes or no, a whole number, a date, one of options you list, or a short code of up to 16 letters, digits, _ or -. It can't give you any other text, such as a title, a name or a sentence: for those, read the item. It asks a question of something your request shows only as a note ("Hidden here as h1: …"), without reading it: a separate model, shown only that and your question, answers in the shape you choose, and you are told only that answer. Using it never stops you doing anything you can do now. Shapes: yes_no; number, a whole number from min to max; day, a date; one_of, one of the options you list (at most 64, each at most 80 characters); token, a short code of at most max (up to 16) characters of A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ and -. The answer may be that the item does not say.

name.description: The name its note gives, such as h1.

question.description: What to ask of the item, in one sentence.

shape.description: The shape the answer is read in.

min.description: For number: the least it may be.

max.description: For number: the most it may be. For token: the most characters it may have.

options.description: For one_of: the options, in order.

tools.name: topic
tools.description: Say which topic the user's latest message is about. Call it once, before answering, when the message says the topic may have changed.

about.description: current: it carries on the current topic. earlier: it goes back to an earlier topic. new: a subject not discussed before.

earlier.description: For earlier: the earlier topic's key, as the note lists them.

name.description: For new: a short name for the subject, at most four words.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file in the checkout. Shows at most 2000 lines and 50 KB, from `offset`; a note after the text says which lines were shown and the offset to continue from. Each line is shown as its number, right-aligned, a tab, then its text, numbered from 1 as `search` numbers them; the number and tab are not part of the file. Fails when the file does not exist, is a directory, is over 16 MB or is not UTF-8, or when `offset` is past its end. A path must be relative to the checkout's root and stay inside it, and may not name a .env file (.env or .env.*); a link that leads outside the checkout or to such a file is refused.

path.description: The file, relative to the checkout's root.

offset.description: The line to start at, counting from 1.

tools.name: list
tools.description: List the files and directories under a directory of the checkout, as paths relative to it, sorted, directories ending in `/`. `depth` 1 lists its own entries; each level more goes one directory deeper. Hidden directories (such as .git) and node_modules, out and target are listed but not entered. Shows at most 2000 lines and 50 KB. Fails when the directory does not exist or is a file. A path must be relative to the checkout's root and stay inside it, and may not name a .env file (.env or .env.*); a link that leads outside the checkout or to such a file is refused.

path.description: The directory, relative to the checkout's root; `.` for the root.

depth.description: How many levels down to list; 1 when not given.

tools.name: search
tools.description: Find the lines matching a Java regular expression in the files under a path of the checkout (a directory, or one file). Each match is shown as `path:line: text`, in path order; a match anywhere in the line counts. Skips .env files, links, hidden directories (such as .git), node_modules, out and target, files over 16 MB and files that are not UTF-8. A line is cut at 500 characters; at most 2000 lines and 50 KB of matches are shown. Says "No matches." when none match. Fails when the pattern is not a valid regular expression or the path does not exist. A path must be relative to the checkout's root and stay inside it, and may not name a .env file (.env or .env.*); a link that leads outside the checkout or to such a file is refused.

path.description: Where to search, relative to the checkout's root; `.` for all of it.

pattern.description: The regular expression, in Java's syntax.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Make `content` the whole of a file in the checkout, creating it and any missing directory above it, or replacing what it held. `content` is the file's text only: never the line numbers and tabs `read` shows. To change part of a file, use `edit`. Fails when the path is a directory or a directory on the way is a file. A path must be relative to the checkout's root and stay inside it, and may not name a .env file (.env or .env.*); a link that leads outside the checkout or to such a file is refused.

path.description: The file, relative to the checkout's root.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Change a file in the checkout by replacing passages of it. Every `oldText` is matched against the file as it was before this call, exactly, whitespace and line breaks included; each must occur exactly once, and no two may overlap. `oldText` and `newText` are the file's text only: leave out the line number and tab `read` shows before each line. All the edits apply, or none does. Line endings (\r\n or \n) and a byte order mark are kept. Fails, naming the edit by its index from 0, when an `oldText` is empty, not found (saying so when it carries `read`'s line numbers), or found more than once, when two edits overlap, or when the edits change nothing; also when the file does not exist, is a directory, is over 16 MB or is not UTF-8. A path must be relative to the checkout's root and stay inside it, and may not name a .env file (.env or .env.*); a link that leads outside the checkout or to such a file is refused.

path.description: The file, relative to the checkout's root.

oldText.description: The exact text to replace, as it is in the file, without `read`'s line numbers.

edits.description: The passages to replace, each found exactly once in the file.

tools.name: run
tools.description:
Run a program from the list below in the checkout's root, with nothing on its input, and return its exit code and its output and errors, interleaved. `program` and `args` are passed as they are, with no shell: no pipes, `&&`, redirects, globs or variables; use `search` and `read` for what those were for. A non-zero exit is returned, not an error. Shows at most the last 2000 lines and 50 KB of output. Give `git commit` its message with `-m`: no editor can open. Waits up to `wait` seconds (30 when not given): a command still running then keeps running, and the answer gives its id and its output so far; follow it with `tail`, or end it with `stop`. At most 4 commands run at once in a checkout. Fails, running nothing, when the command is not on the list or 4 are already running, and when it cannot start. A command is killed with everything it started when it runs past `timeout` (at most 1800 seconds, and that when not given) or its output passes 16 MB. The commands it runs, where `…` stands for any further arguments:
- `git status …`
- `git diff …`
- `git log …`
- `git show …`
- `git add …`
- `git commit …`
- `./mill …`
- `scripts/check …` (at least one argument: the suites or modules to check)

args.description: Its arguments, in order, each passed as one word.

wait.description: The most seconds to wait for it to end before answering with its id; 30 when not given.

program.description: The program, written as the list writes it.

timeout.description: The most seconds it may run, waited on or not; 1800 when not given.

tools.name: tail
tools.description: See how a command `run` left running stands: still running, with its output so far, or ended, with its exit code and output. Give `wait` to wait up to that many seconds for it to end; the answer comes as soon as it does. Shows at most the last 2000 lines and 50 KB of output; when that cuts it, the answer names the file holding all of it, for `read`. Fails when no command with that id is kept in this checkout: grit restarted since it started, or it ended and was forgotten after 8 newer commands ended; and when its output passed 16 MB, which killed it.

id.description: The id `run` answered with, such as `3f9a2c1e`.

wait.description: The most seconds to wait for it to end; 0 when not given.

tools.name: stop
tools.description: End a command `run` left running, killing it and everything it started, and return its output until then. A command that already ended is left as it was, and its exit code and output returned. Fails as `tail` does when no command with that id is kept.

id.description: The id `run` answered with, such as `3f9a2c1e`.

tools.name: scout_show
tools.description:
Name the member you need (`Owner.member`), and pass `body` with its name for its body, rather than showing a whole object; pass every symbol you need in one call. With a short name several definitions share, pass the full name.

To read or call a definition: its signature and Scaladoc, with one-line outlines of the project types it names. Pass every symbol you need in one call. Each definition's NN-MM header, and each outline, ends with its size, `[N.N KB]`; a class, trait, object or enum shown without its body ends with its closing lines, an anchor for an Edit adding a member to it. After them, one line per named symbol counts the tests in test sources that exercise it: `-- tests of <Sym>: N in M suites (nearest: A, B, C); …`, the line ending with a hint to list them, which over MCP is `tests` set to `list`; N the tests holding a reference to it or to a member, M the suites holding one in a test or a helper, and the nearest at most three of those suites, the ones under the symbol's own module directory first, then those holding the most references; `-- tests of <Sym>: none name it …` when no suite holds one, saying what is not counted (a call through a supertype's member it overrides, a subtype's own members), and `no test names it; helpers in M suites do` when only helpers outside every test hold one. With `tests` set to `list`, a Tests section lists them instead: a `## tests exercising <Sym>` line, then per file a `== file  package` line and entries `NN-MM <Suite>: <test name>`, or `NN-MM <Suite>: helper <def>` for a helper holding a reference itself. Those lines are not file text. A name main sources lack is looked up in test sources, under a `-- in test sources: <full name>` note, with no tests line. A short name several definitions end with picks the one outside test sources and the `secondary` paths `.outline.conf` names, when only one is, under a note naming the others; otherwise every one is shown, under an `-- ambiguous` note listing each as `find` does.

Answers come from the module's last compile: compile it with the project's build after you edit it, and before your first question when you don't know that its compiled output is current (a new worktree, a branch just switched, pulled or rebased, files changed by another session).

Example: {"symbols":["Ledger.post"],"body":["post"]}

body.description: Member names of the definitions shown, their simple names; there is no `all` or `full`. A path reaches a nested member (`Settling.began`), printed whole under its owner-qualified name; a bare name none of a shown type's own members has is looked for in its nested owners, printed when one owner has it and named with each owner when several do. A member of an anonymous class (`new T { … }`) in the body of a val or def shown, or among a shown type's members, prints as file text under its class's name, as `Shelf.of (anonymous).holds`; a name defined there only as a local is named with its line and the option that prints that body whole. A name a shown type lacks that another type's member has, with the shown type in its signature (`Place`, body `readsFrom`, defined as `Tx.readsFrom(source: Place)`), is named with its file, lines and signature and the show printing it; with no such member, the note names the find listing every definition of the name. A JSON array of strings, e.g. ["post"].

docs.description: print every member's doc whole; without it, a member of a shown type not named in `body` prints its doc's first sentence only.

depth.description: how many levels of project types to outline under the named ones: 0, 1 or 2; default 1.

tests.description: `summary` (the default: the count line), `list` (every test and helper exercising the named symbols, in place of the count line) or `none` (neither the count line nor the list).

max_kb.description: cut the answer at N KB (1024 bytes), a whole number from 1; default 12. It cuts whole entries, never inside one, and a cut answer ends with a `-- cut at N KB` line giving the max_kb that shows it all, or narrow the query. In show, a type of two members or more is cut between its members, its head first, then the members `body` names, then the rest in file order; what `body` names prints whatever N. A cut type's answer ends with a `-- cut at N KB after <member>` line, with a hint to rerun with a larger max_kb or to pass `body` for one member (the hint only without `body`); its closing lines print only when no member was cut.

private.description: include private members. Ask for them only to edit them or to understand an implementation; otherwise trust the public interface and referential transparency to understand the code. Name the members you need with `body`; with no `body`, `private` on a whole type lists every internal helper.

symbols.description: Symbols to show, each Name, Name.member or fully qualified. A JSON array of strings, e.g. ["Ledger.post"].

To implement or change a trait: its implementations (private ones, and anonymous classes named by the definition holding them, as `Shelf.of (anonymous)`), contracts and their suites, each definition's line ending with its size, `[N.N KB]`; the trait, and with `member` its member shown without its body when that member is a type, ends with its closing lines.

trait.description: the trait or abstract class, by name; a short name several definitions end with means its one candidate outside test and secondary sources, as in show, and with none or several the answer lists each, picking none: name one fully. A name that is no trait or abstract class, such as an opaque type, answers what it is and the show and uses for it.

tools.name: scout_uses
tools.description:
Every reference to a definition, before changing it; use this, not grep. With a short name several definitions share, pass the full name: a short name may resolve to one of them. It takes `sites` (every site listed), `in` and `outside` (narrow by path); it has no `private` parameter.

Sites are grouped by file (`== file`), then by the definition holding them: an `in <owner>` line (the member around the site, or `<Suite>: <test name>` for a site in a test) ending with the owner's size, `[N.N KB]`, then each site as `<line>  <source line>`, and last `[N sites in M files]`. Over 20 sites in all, each file prints as `== file  N sites` and each owner once as `in <owner>  N sites`, with no site lines, ending `-- N sites in M files`, with a hint to list them all by `sites`, or to narrow by `in` or `outside`.

Answers come from the module's last compile: compile it with the project's build after you edit it, and before your first question when you don't know that its compiled output is current (a new worktree, a branch just switched, pulled or rebased, files changed by another session).

target. Where it is silent, use your judgement. If the brief's premise is wrong (a name that does

## Before anything else

`CLAUDE.md` summarises every style rule. From `STYLE.md` read only rule 10 (the elision test,
and what a doc must and must not say) and the Tests section; open another rule's section only
when a change turns on it. `docs/capture-checking.md` has every compile trap met so far: search
it for the error when one appears, rather than reading it up front. Read the module README for
the package you touch. Never read `.env`. Make no model call.

## Reading and editing code

Read Scala through scout's tools (`scout_find`, `scout_show`, `scout_uses`, `scout_file` and the
rest you are offered), not by reading whole `.scala` files. If `.claude/rules/reading-scala.md`
exists, read it before your first query: where it names a tool `mcp__scout__show`, use
`scout_show`, and so on for each. scout answers from compiled output, and this checkout starts
with none: compile the module you ask about first (`./mill <module>.compile`, through `run`),
and again after you edit it. Change files with `edit` (exact text) or `write` (a new file).

## Rules

- **This directory only.** There is no worktree to make, no other branch, no planning store, no
  main session or manager, and no GitHub. Where the brief names any of them, read it as this
  directory and the branch `bench`. Never push and never rewrite history.
- **Commands.** `run` starts only the programs its description lists, with no shell. A
  command that is refused will be refused again: find another way. A build or a test run can
  take minutes: when `run` answers with an id, follow it with `tail` rather than starting it
  again.
- **Stay in scope.** Ideas outside the brief go in your last message, not the code.
- **Recorded data.** A change to a workflow step's name, order, or any recorded output encoding
  must replay every history (ADR 0004; `TurnReplayTests` is the gate).

## Build and verify

- Types over comments: turn a doc-stated invariant into a type (private constructor, smart
  constructor, ADT shaped by case); don't restate what a type or visibility says; do state
  failure modes and behaviour-changing constants.
- **Red first.** Each new behaviour's test is seen red for the right reason, an assertion
  failure and not a compile error, before its code.
- **Checks cost real time.** While editing, compile, don't test: after each burst of edits,
  `./mill <module>.compile`. Run a test only to see it red or green (`scripts/check <Suite>`).
  Run the module's check once per commit, when its edits are done. The checks the task is held
  to run after you stop.
- **A new unit test is fast.** One over 5 s is a defect.
- Commit in the repository's message style (see `git log`), one item per commit, on `bench`.

## When done

End with a short message: each commit's hash and subject, the tests you added and their reds,
the judgement calls you made, and anything you left undone.
